result.summary: The Pythia prays, enters Apollo's shrine at Delphi, and returns horrified at the sight of a bloodstained suppliant and sleeping Furies. Apollo promises Orestes protection and sends him with Hermes to Athens. Clytaemestra's ghost then rouses the sleeping Furies to chase him.

scenes.title: Prefatory notes and argument
scenes.summary: Setting, date and an argument summarizing the whole play.

scenes.title: The Prophetess's prayer
scenes.summary: The priestess recounts the line of gods who held the Delphic oracle and invokes them before taking her seat.

scenes.title: The priestess sees horrors
scenes.summary: She comes out terrified, describing a bloody suppliant and a throng of hideous sleeping women.
scenes.stakes: The priestess is overcome by fear and frailty.

scenes.title: Apollo sends Orestes away
scenes.summary: Apollo promises protection, tells Orestes to flee to Athens and clasp Athena's image, and charges Hermes to guide him.
scenes.stakes: Orestes is hunted by the Furies and needs release from his pollution.

scenes.title: Clytaemestra's ghost rouses Furies
scenes.summary: The ghost reproaches the sleeping Furies for letting Orestes escape and urges them to wake.
scenes.stakes: Clytaemestra is dishonoured among the dead and her vengeance is lost.

alias_notes.explanation: A cult title of Apollo as spokesman of Zeus.
Said here to take his name from Phoebe.

notable_quotes.reason: The priestess states that her prophecy follows the god's lead.
A striking claim that the sleeping mind sees more clearly than the waking one.

analysis.text: The opening sets the old, vengeful order of the Furies against the newer Olympian order of Apollo, preparing the move from blood-vengeance to law.
The Pythia's list of Delphi's divine owners reflects the city's claim to ancient, peaceful succession of its oracle, and the play was staged in 458 B.C.

fun_facts.text: The Eumenides is the last play of the Oresteia, the only surviving complete Greek tragic trilogy.

language_notes.text: The City Dionysia was Athens' spring festival of Dionysus, where tragedies were performed in competition before the citizens.
Erinyes are the avenging spirits (Furies) who pursue those who shed kindred blood.
A suppliant is one who seeks protection at a sacred place, which made him inviolable.
Pallas is another name for Athena, here used as her title.
"Blood-kin" means related by blood; the argument turns on whether a mother counts as a true blood relative of her child.
The Hill of Ares is the Areopagus in Athens, where the court of homicide sat; the Erinyes are given a shrine beneath it.
"Took second this oracular seat of her mother" means Themis received the oracle as the second holder, inheriting it from her mother Earth.
Phoebus ("bright one") is Apollo's title; the text links it to Phoebe's name, a play on the name rather than a strict etymology.
"Pallas' ship-frequented shores" refers to Attica, land of Athena (Pallas), where Apollo landed on his way from Delos to Delphi.
Hephaestus' children are the Athenians, who road-building Apollo's journey; they cleared a route for his procession to Delphi.
"Loxias" is a cult title of Apollo, linked to his oracular, obscure speech. "Stablished" means established.
Bromius ("roaring one") is Dionysus. Pentheus, king of Thebes, resisted his worship and was torn apart by Bacchants, here compared to a hunted hare.
Consultants entered "by lot": the order of those seeking the oracle was decided by drawing lots.
Loxias is a title of Apollo, god of Delphi, whose oracle the priestess serves. 'House' means his temple.
The 'centre-stone' is the omphalos, the navel-stone marking Delphi as the center of the world.
'Suppliants' are people who seek protection or purification at a sacred place.
Gorgons were monstrous winged women with snakes for hair, whose gaze turned people to stone; Medusa was one.
Phineus was a king tormented by the Harpies, winged creatures that snatched or fouled his food. She had seen them in paintings.
'Puissant' means powerful; 'purgeth' is archaic for 'purges', meaning cleanses.
"Beldames" are old women, often hags; the phrase "aged children" is a paradox, since the Furies are ancient yet childlike in mind.
Tartarus is the deepest part of the underworld, a gloomy pit below Hades where the Furies dwell.
"Pallas' burgh" is Athens, city of Pallas Athena; her "ancient image" is her old wooden statue on the Acropolis, where suppliants could seek protection.
"Judges of thy cause" anticipates the trial Athena will set up at Athens; "at my behest" means Apollo commanded the matricide.
Orestes urges Apollo not to forget him: knowing himself righteous, Apollo must also care for, not neglect, his suppliant.
The footnote marks a pun: Hermes is the "Conductor" (Greek hegemonios), the god who guides travellers and souls.
"Because of him I slew" means because of Orestes' act of killing her; the dead reproach her for a murder left unavenged.
She means that in sleep the mind sees truly, as in dreams, while waking people cannot foresee their fate.
"Wineless libations" are offerings of water, honey and milk, poured to the Furies instead of wine; "sober appeasement" means a calming gift.
"An hour unshared by any god" means a night hour when no Olympian receives worship, so the offerings belonged to the Furies alone.
"Dragoness" refers to the Furies, here imagined as serpent-like; "travail" means toil, so sleep and weariness are called conspirators.

context_notes.text: The heroic age is the legendary era of Greek heroes, after the gods' rule and before recorded history, when the Trojan War took place.
Clytaemestra killed her husband Agamemnon on his return from Troy; her son Orestes later killed her to avenge him.
The Areopagus was historically Athens' court for homicide; Aeschylus gives it a mythic origin in Athena's founding.
Athena's casting vote for acquittal in a tied ballot reflected the Athenian principle that a tie favoured the accused.
Earth (Gaia) and Themis, goddess of established right, are the first two holders of the Delphic oracle in this legendary succession.
Delos was Apollo's birthplace island; Parnassus is the mountain above Delphi, site of his oracle.
Delphus is the legendary eponymous king of the region, from whom Delphi was said to take its name.
The Corycian cave on Parnassus was sacred to the Nymphs and Pan, near Delphi.
Pleistus is the river of the Delphi area. Zeus the Fulfiller (Teleios) is the god who brings prayers and plans to completion.
The olive branch wrapped in wool was the traditional sign of a suppliant seeking protection. Blood on his hands and sword shows he has just killed.
These sleeping women are the Furies, ancient goddesses who pursue those who shed kindred blood. Here they hound Orestes.
Apollo, god of prophecy, had ordered Orestes to avenge his father Agamemnon by killing his mother Clytemnestra, and now protects him at Delphi.
The Furies are ancient avenging goddesses who pursue those who shed kindred blood; here they sleep inside Apollo's temple.
Hermes is Apollo's half-brother, both being sons of Zeus (here sometimes Jove), and is the divine messenger and guide of travellers.
Clytaemestra was killed by her son Orestes in revenge for her murder of Agamemnon, his father. The Furies pursue those who shed kindred blood.
Orestes has fled to Athens after being purified at Delphi by Apollo, who protects him.
The Furies, goddesses of the underworld, avenge murder within the family, which is why Clytaemestra appeals to them.

literary_notes.text: The sleeping, fearsome Erinyes create a vivid, eerie opening image of guilt that pursues relentlessly yet is momentarily exhausted.
The Erinyes' change from Spirits of Wrath to Spirits of Blessing (Eumenides) resolves the play, symbolizing vengeance giving way to civic justice.
The priestess's careful, pious ordering of the gods establishes her reverent character and the oracle's legitimate, peaceful lineage.
Apollo as mere spokesman of Zeus introduces the play's theme of Zeus's supreme authority behind Apollo's later actions.
Her hope for good fortune beyond past visits anticipates the terrifying sight inside the temple that she is about to meet.
The aged priestess compares herself to a child, conveying how fear has stripped her of strength and dignity.
She names the women, then retracts it. The self-correction shows her struggle to find words for something beyond ordinary experience.
Snorting breath and oozing rheum create a repulsive sensory picture of the Furies, stressing their foulness.
She praises Apollo as healer and purifier of houses, while the polluted Orestes and the monstrous Furies already sit in his shrine.
"Aged children" joins opposites to show the Furies as primitive, ancient beings, and to mark Apollo's contempt for them.
The pursuit across continent, sea and island cities stresses the Furies' relentlessness and the long wandering Orestes faces.
Hermes is compared to a shepherd guiding Orestes, showing gentle, watchful care for the vulnerable suppliant.
The ghost's bitter command to sleep on mocks the Furies, who are supposed to be tireless pursuers.
The ghost points to the wounds in her heart, a vivid image that supports her claim to vengeance.
Orestes is compared to a fawn bounding free of a snare, casting the Furies as hunters and him as hunted prey.
Slumber and travail are treated as conspirators who have defeated the Furies' power, blaming the sleep itself.
